Course Objectives
Sr. 
No. Objectives
The course aims:
1
To introduce advanced concepts of transaction management and recovery techniques.
2
To impart knowledge related to query processing and query optimizer phases of a database 
management system
3
To introduce concepts of advanced access control techniques like role based and discretionary 
methods 
4
To introduce advanced database models like distributed databases and emerging data models 
like temporal, mobile and spatial databases. 
5
To introduce the concepts of Big Data technologies and frameworks used to store, process and 
analyze large-scale datasets for strategic decision making.
Course Outcomes
The student will be able to:
1
Explain and analyze the concept of a transaction, and evaluate how ACID properties are 
preserved during concurrent transactions in a database
2
Measure and evaluate query costs, and design alternative efficient paths for optimized query 
execution
3 Apply and integrate advanced access control protocols to regulate and secure database usage
4
Create distributed database models and understand design of applications using advanced 
paradigms such as mobile and spatial databases

5
Understand Big Data concepts and explain technologies such as Hadoop, HDFS, MapReduce, 
Spark and NoSQL databases used for large-scale data processing and analytics.

3.1 Advanced Database Access protocols: Discretionary Access Control Based 
on Granting and Revoking Privileges; 
07

access protocol.
3.3 SQL Injection; Introduction to Statistical Database Security, Introduction to 
flow control
4.0
Distributed Databases 
4.1 Introduction: Distributed Data Processing, What is a Distributed Database 
System? Design Issues. Distributed DBMS Architecture. Distributed 
Database Design, Data Fragmentation & Allocation in distributed databases.
Overview of Query Processing and Query Optimization in Distributed 
Databases;

Databases; Overview of Concurrency Control and Recovery in 
Distributed Databases.
4.3 Overview of Advanced Database models like Mobile databases, Temporal

Introduction to Big Data

5.1 Introduction to Big Data; Characteristics of Big Data (Volume, Velocity, 
Variety, Veracity, Value); Sources of Big Data; Traditional Data vs Big Data; 
Applications of Big Data in various domains such as healthcare, banking, social 
media and e-commerce.
08

Distributed File System (HDFS); MapReduce Framework; YARN

5.3 Introduction to Big Data Processing Frameworks; Apache Spark Overview; 
NoSQL Databases – Key-Value Stores, Column-Oriented Databases, 
Document Databases, Graph Databases; Applications of Big Data Analytics 
in Business Intelligence and Decision Support Systems.

MODULE 1: 
Transactions Management, 
Concurrency and Recovery
PART 1- TRANSACTIONS
MS. ALVINA LOPES

Contents
❖ Transaction Concept 
❖ Transaction State 
❖ Implementation of Atomicity and Durability 
❖ Concurrent Executions 
❖ Serializability 
❖ Recoverability 
❖ Implementation of Isolation
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 2

Transaction Concept
❖ Transaction is a collection of operation that form a single logical unit.
❖ Transaction is a unit of program execution that access and possibly 
update various data items.
❖ Transaction is an event that occurs in the database.
❖ Transaction reads a value from the database or write a values to the 
database.
❖ Transaction also performs group of task.
❖ Eg., A bank employee transfers $5000 from B’s Account to X’s Account.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 3

Transaction Concept
❖ A transaction must see a consistent database.
❖ During transaction execution the database may be inconsistent.
❖ When the transaction is committed, the database must be 
consistent.
❖ Two main issues to deal with:
❖ Failures of various kinds, such as hardware failures and system 
crashes
❖ Concurrent execution of multiple transactions.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 4

Transaction Concept 
Key Points:
• Consistency: Consistency means database remains in a valid state before and 
after a transaction. 
• Integrity: Integrity means the accuracy and correctness of data stored in the 
database. It ensures that all data follows defined rules and constraints such as 
primary key, foreign key, and domain constraints. 
• Reliability: Reliability means the ability of the database system to function 
correctly even in the presence of failures such as system crashes, power 
failures, or errors.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 5

Basic Database Access Operations 
1. Read / Access Data (R)
It is the operation of reading data from 
the database.
Data is fetched from disk (database 
storage)
Stored temporarily in a memory 
variable
Used when we want to view or use data
Example:
Reading account balance from database
2. Write / Change Data (W)
It is the operation of updating data in the 
database.
Data is taken from memory variable
Written back to disk (database)
Used when we want to modify data
Example:
Updating balance after deposit
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 6

Basic Database Access Operations 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 7
4. Rollback
Rollback is a Transaction Control 
Language (TCL) command.
It undoes all changes made in a 
transaction
Restores the database to the previous 
state
Used when an error occurs or 
transaction fails
Marks unsuccessful completion of 
transaction
3. Commit
Commit is a Transaction Control 
Language (TCL) command.
It permanently saves all changes
made in a transaction 
After commit, changes cannot be 
undone
Marks successful completion of 
transaction

Transaction Concept Contd
Example (Bank Transaction)
A bank employee transfers ₹50 from Account B to Account X
This transaction includes:
Read balance of B 
Deduct ₹50 from B 
Read balance of X 
Add ₹50 to X 
All steps must happen together — otherwise it causes inconsistency.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 8

Example Contd
Transfer of 50₹ from Account A to Account B.
Initially A= 500₹, B= 800₹. 
This data is brought to RAM from Hard Disk.
 R(A) -- 500 // Accessed from RAM.
 A = A-50 // Deducting 50₹ from A.
 W(A)--450 // Updated in RAM.
 R(B) -- 800 // Accessed from RAM.
 B=B+50 // 50₹ is added to B's Account.
 W(B) --850 // Updated in RAM.
commit // The data in RAM is taken back to Hard Disk.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 9

Stages of Transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 10

Transaction Concept (CONTD)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 11
• The database starts in a consistent 
state before the transaction 
begins.
• During execution, it may become 
temporarily inconsistent.
• All operations are performed 
within the transaction.
• After completion (COMMIT), the 
database returns to a consistent 
state.

Transaction State Diagram
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 12
Success path:
Active → Partially Committed → Committed
Failure path:
Active → Failed → Aborted

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
Example :
Transfer ₹5000 from Account A to Account B
1. Active State
• Transaction is currently executing
• Performing operations like read/write
Example:
Read balance of A 
Deduct ₹5000 
Add ₹5000 to B 
Transaction is in progress
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 13

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
2. Partially Committed State
• All operations are executed
• But changes are not yet permanently saved
Example:
₹5000 deducted from A 
₹5000 added to B 
Waiting to execute COMMIT
Almost complete, but not final
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 14

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
3. Committed State
• Changes are permanently saved in database
• Transaction is successful
Example:
Money successfully transferred 
Data stored permanently 
Cannot be undone now
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 15

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
4. Failed State
• Transaction cannot continue
• Due to error, crash, or invalid operation
Example:
System crashes after deducting money from A 
Network failure occurs 
Transaction stops
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 16

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
5. Aborted State
• All changes are undone (ROLLBACK)
• Database returns to its state prior to the start of the transaction.
• Two options:
• restart the transaction – only if no internal logical error
• kill the transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 17

Transaction State Diagram (CONTD)
5. Aborted State
Example:
₹5000 deducted from A is restored 
No money transferred 
No partial update remains
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 18

Transaction Property
❖To ensure integrity of data, the database system must ensure:
1. Atomicity
2. Consistency
3. Isolation and
4. Durability
❖ Also, known as ACID Properties.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 19

1.Atomicity
• A transaction should be atomic, meaning it is executed completely or not at all. 
• A transaction cannot be executed partially. 
• Either all operations of the transaction are properly reflected in the database or none are.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 20

2. Consistency
• Consistency ensures that the database remains in a valid state before and 
after a transaction. 
• A valid state follows all rules, constraints, and relationships (primary key, 
foreign key, etc.). 
• Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves the consistency of the 
database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 21

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 22
• The diagram shows a transaction transferring ₹100 from account X to account Y.
• X is reduced by 100 and Y is increased by 100.
• The total balance (i.e 700) remains unchanged, maintaining consistency.

3. Isolation
• Isolation ensures that transactions execute independently without interfering with 
each other. 
• Changes made by one transaction are not visible to others until they are committed. 
• It ensures that concurrent transactions give the same result as serial execution. 
Example
Two users updating the same account:
One transaction should not see partial changes of another. Ensures correct and 
independent execution
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 23

Durability
• Durability ensures that once a transaction is committed, its changes are permanently 
stored in the database, even if a system crash or failure occurs.
• After a transaction commits, the data is written to non-volatile storage (disk). 
• Even if the system crashes immediately after commit, the database can recover the 
committed data using logs or backups. 
• No committed data will be lost. 
Example:
After transferring money from Account A to Account B:
The updated balances are saved on disk. 
Even if the system crashes right after commit, the transaction remains intact after 
recovery.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 24

ACID Properties- Example of Fund Transfer
• Transaction to transfer $50 from account A to account B: 
1. read(A) 
2. A := A – 50 
3. write(A) 
4. read(B) 
5. B := B + 50 
6. write(B)
• Consistency requirement – the sum of A and B is unchanged by the execution of the 
transaction.
• Atomicity requirement — if the transaction fails after step 3 and before step 6, the 
system should ensure that its updates are not reflected in the database, else an 
inconsistency will result.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 25

ACID Properties- Example of Fund Transfer
• Durability requirement — once the user has been notified that the transaction has 
completed (i.e., the transfer of the $50 has taken place), the updates to the database 
by the transaction must persist despite failures.
• Isolation requirement — if between steps 3 and 6, another transaction is allowed to 
access the partially updated database, it will see an inconsistent database (the sum A + 
B will be less than it should be).
• Can be ensured trivially by running transactions serially, that is one after the other. 
• However, executing multiple transactions concurrently has significant benefits, as we will see.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 26

Implementation of Atomicity and 
Durability
❖The recovery-management component of a database system implements the 
support for atomicity and durability.
❖The shadow-database scheme:
➢assume that only one transaction is active at a time.
➢a pointer called db_pointer always points to the current consistent copy of 
the database.
➢all updates are made on a shadow copy of the database, and db_pointer is 
made to point to the updated shadow copy only after the transaction 
reaches partial commit and all updated pages have been flushed to disk.
➢in case transaction fails, old consistent copy pointed to by db_pointer can 
be used, and the shadow copy can be deleted.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 27

Implementation of Atomicity and 
Durability
The shadow-database scheme:
• Assumes disks to not fail.
• Useful for text editors, but extremely inefficient for large databases: executing 
a single transaction requires copying the entire database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 28

Concurrent Executions
❖ Multiple transactions are allowed to run concurrently in the system.
❖ Advantages are:
❖improved throughput and increased processor and disk utilization, leading 
to better transaction throughput: one transaction can be using the CPU 
while another is reading from or writing to the disk 
❖Reduced waiting time and reduced average response time for transactions: 
short transactions need not wait behind long ones.
❖ Concurrency control schemes – mechanisms to achieve isolation, i.e., to 
control the interaction among the concurrent transactions in order to prevent 
them from destroying the consistency of the database.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 29

Schedule
A schedule is an ordered sequence of operations (read, write, commit, etc.) from 
one or more transactions, representing how the transactions are executed in the 
database system.
Key Points
A schedule determines the execution order of operations from multiple 
transactions 
It can include: 
◦ Operations of a single transaction, or 
◦ Interleaved operations of multiple transactions 
It preserves the order of operations within each transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 30
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 31

Serial Schedules in DBMS
❖A serial schedule is a schedule in which transactions are executed one after 
another, without any interleaving of operations.
❖Only one transaction executes at a time
❖The next transaction starts only after the previous one finishes
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 32

Serial Schedules in DBMS
Key Characteristics
Serial schedules are always:
Consistent
→ Database remains correct because there is no interference between 
transactions 
Recoverable
→ A transaction commits only after the transactions it depends on have 
committed 
Cascadeless
→ No transaction reads uncommitted data, so no cascading rollback
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 33

Serial Schedules in DBMS
Problems with Serial Scheduling
Although serial schedules are safe and simple, they have several performance 
drawbacks:
1. More Waiting Time
2. Less Resource Utilization
3. Less Throughput
4. Late Response Time
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 34

Examples of Serial Schedules
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 35

Non-Serial Schedule 
A non-serial schedule is a schedule in which multiple transactions execute 
concurrently, and their operations are interleaved (mixed) with each other.
Key Characteristics
Non-serial schedules are NOT always: Consistent, Recoverable, Cascadeless.
Advantages
Reduced Waiting Time: Transactions do not wait for others to complete 
Increased Resource Utilization: CPU, memory, and I/O are used efficiently 
Decreased Response Time: Faster execution for individual transactions 
Higher Throughput: More transactions completed per unit time 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 36

Examples of Non-Serial Schedules
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 37

Concurrent Executions
•Concurrent execution means that multiple transactions are executed 
simultaneously in an interleaved(one after other) manner, rather than one 
transaction completing before another begins.
•When multiple transactions execute concurrently without proper control, it 
may lead to problems affecting data integrity and consistency. Such issues are 
called Concurrency Problems (or Anomalies)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 38

Concurrency Problems
1. Lost Update (Write–Write Conflict)
2. Uncommitted Data / Dirty Read (Write–Read Conflict)
3. Inconsistent Retrieval / Unrepeatable Read (Read–Write Conflict)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 39

Concurrent Executions
Solution
To ensure correctness, DBMS enforces:
Serializability
Concurrent schedule must produce the same result as some serial schedule
Concurrency Control Techniques
•Locking (2PL – Two Phase Locking) 
•Timestamp Ordering 
•Validation-based protocols
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 40

Serializability
•Serializability is a concept in DBMS that ensures that even when transactions are 
executed concurrently (non-serially), the final result is equivalent to some serial 
(one-by-one) execution, thus maintaining a consistent database.
There are two ways to check whether any non-serial schedule is serializable.
1. Conflict Serializability
2. View Serializability
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 41

Types of Serializability
1. Conflict Serializability
A schedule is said to be conflict serializable if it can be converted into a serial 
schedule by swapping only non-conflicting operations, without changing the 
effect of the schedule.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 42

Types of Serializability
Conflict Serializability
Two operations conflict if:
• They belong to different transactions, and 
• They operate on the same data item, and 
• At least one of them is a write (W) operation.
Types of Conflicts
•Read–Write (R–W)
•Write–Read (W–R)
•Write–Write (W–W)
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 43

Precedence Graph (Serialization Graph)
A precedence graph is a directed graph used to determine whether a schedule is 
conflict serializable.
Steps to Check Conflict Serializability
Create Nodes
◦ For each transaction 𝑇𝑖
 ,create a node (vertex) in the graph 
Add Edges
◦ For every conflicting operation pair, draw a directed edge 𝑇𝑖 → 𝑇𝑗
if an operation of 𝑇𝑖 occurs before a conflicting operation of 𝑇𝑗
Check for Cycles
◦ No Cycle → Schedule is Conflict Serializable
◦ Cycle Present → Schedule is Not Conflict Serializable
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 44

Precedence Graph (CONTD)
Important Rules for Edges (Very Important )
Draw edge Ti → Tj if:
Read–Write (R–W)
Tj writes after Ti reads 
Write–Read (W–R)
Tj reads after Ti writes 
Write–Write (W–W)
Tj writes after Ti writes 
These rules come directly from conflict conditions

View Serializability
A schedule is said to be view serializable if it is view equivalent to some serial 
schedule.
View Equivalent Schedules
Two schedules (one serial and one non-serial) are said to be view equivalent if 
they satisfy the following conditions:
1. Initial Read: If a transaction reads the initial value of a data item in one 
schedule,
it must read the initial value in the other schedule also. 
2. Read-From Relationship: If a transaction reads a value written by another 
transaction, it must read from the same transaction in both schedules. 
3. Final Write: The last write operation on each data item must be done by the 
same transaction in both schedules.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 54

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 55
Two schedules S1 and S2 are view equivalent if:
1. Initial Read Condition
If a transaction reads the initial value of a data item in S1,
it must read the initial value in S2 also. 
2. Read-From Condition (Very Important )
If a transaction Ti reads a value written by Tj in S1,
then in S2 also, Ti must read from Tj
3. Final Write Condition
The last write on each data item must be done by the same transaction in both 
schedules. 
Schedules S1 and S2 are said to be view equivalent if they have the same initial reads, the 
same read-from relationships, and the same final write operations on all data items.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 56
INITIAL READ
•In schedule S, transaction T1 performs R(A) before any write operation on A, so 
it reads the initial value of A. 
•However, in schedule S′, transaction T2 performs W(A) before T1 reads A, so T1 
reads the value written by T2 instead of the initial value. 
•This violates the initial read condition of view equivalence, which requires that 
a transaction must read the same initial value in both schedules. 
•Therefore, schedules S and S′ are not view equivalent.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 57
Updated Read:
•In schedule S, transaction T2 writes the value of B, and then transaction T3 reads B, so T3 reads 
the value written by T2. 
•However, in schedule S′, the order of operations changes, but T3 still reads B after T2 writes it, 
meaning T3 reads the value written by T2 in both schedules. 
•Since the read-from relationship (i.e., which transaction writes and which transaction reads) is 
preserved in both schedules, the read-from condition is satisfied.
•Therefore, with respect to updated read (read-from condition), schedules S and S′ are view 
equivalent.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 58
Final Write / Final Update
•In schedule S, transaction T1 first writes A, followed by T2 reading A, and finally transaction T3 
performs the last write on A. 
•In schedule S′, although the order of operations is different, the final write on data item A is still 
performed by transaction T3. 
•Since the final write on A is carried out by the same transaction (T3) in both schedules, the final 
write condition is satisfied. 
•Therefore, schedules S and S′ are view equivalent with respect to the final update condition.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 59

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 60
Original Schedule (S)
This is interleaved (mixed)
Step1: Identify Read-From Relations
Check who reads from whom:
•T2 reads A after T1 writes A → T2 depends on T1 
•T2 reads B after T1 writes B → T2 depends on T1
Step2: Check Final Writes
•Final write on A → T2
•Final write on B → T2

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol 
• Two-phase locking does not ensure freedom from deadlocks.
• In addition to deadlocks, there is a possibility of starvation.
• Extensions to basic two-phase locking needed to ensure recoverability of freedom 
from cascading roll-back.

commits/aborts.
• Ensures recoverability and avoids cascading roll-backs
• Rigorous two-phase locking: a transaction must hold all locks till commit/abort. 
• Transactions can be serialized in the order in which they commit.
• Most databases implement rigorous two-phase locking, but refer to it as simply 
two-phase locking.

Timestamp-Based Protocols
•Timestamp-based protocols are concurrency control techniques that use timestamps instead 
of locks to ensure correct execution of transactions. Each transaction is assigned a unique 
timestamp when it starts, which determines its order.
•In the Timestamp Ordering Protocol, all operations must follow the chronological order of 
timestamps. If a transaction tries to read or write a data item in a way that violates this order, 
the transaction is rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp.
•This protocol maintains two timestamps for each data item: read timestamp (RTS) and write 
timestamp (WTS). These are used to decide whether an operation is allowed or should be 
rejected.
•The main advantage of timestamp-based protocols is that they are deadlock-free, since 
transactions do not wait for locks. However, they may lead to frequent rollbacks, which can 
reduce performance in high-contention systems.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 25

Timestamp-Based Protocols
• Each transaction is issued a timestamp when it enters the system. 
• If an old transaction Ti has time-stamp TS(Ti), a new transaction Tj is assigned time￾stamp TS(Tj) such that TS(Ti) <TS(Tj). 
• The protocol manages concurrent execution such that the time-stamps determine the 
serializability order.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 26

Timestamp-Based Protocols
• In order to assure such behavior, the protocol maintains for each data Q two 
timestamp values:
• W-timestamp(Q) is the largest time-stamp of any transaction that executed write(Q) 
successfully.
• R-timestamp(Q) is the largest time-stamp of any transaction that executed read(Q) 
successfully.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 27

Timestamp-Based Protocols
• The timestamp ordering protocol ensures that any conflicting read and write 
operations are executed in timestamp order.
• Suppose a transaction Ti issues a read(Q):
1. If TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), then Ti needs to read a value of Q that was already 
overwritten. Hence, the read operation is rejected, and Ti is rolled back.
2. If TS(Ti)  W-timestamp(Q), then the read operation is executed, and R￾timestamp(Q) is set to max(R-timestamp(Q), TS(Ti)).
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 28

Timestamp-Based Protocols
•Suppose a transaction Ti issues a write(Q):
1. If TS(Ti) < R-timestamp(Q), then the value of Q that Ti is producing was needed 
previously, and the system assumed that that value would never be produced. 
Hence, the write operation is rejected, and Ti is rolled back.
2. If TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), then Ti is attempting to write an obsolete value of 
Q. Hence, this write operation is rejected, and Ti is rolled back.
3. Otherwise, the write operation is executed, and W-timestamp(Q) is set to TS(Ti).

• Modified version of the timestamp-ordering protocol in which obsolete write
operations may be ignored under certain circumstances.
• When Ti attempts to write data item Q, if TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q), then Ti is

Validation-Based Protocol
• Execution of transaction Ti is done in three phases.
1. Read and execution phase: Transaction Ti writes only to temporary local variables
2. Validation phase: Transaction Ti performs a ''validation test'' to determine if local 
variables can be written without violating serializability.
3. Write phase: If Ti is validated, the updates are applied to the database; otherwise, Ti 
is rolled back.

• The three phases of concurrently executing transactions can be interleaved, but each 
transaction must go through the three phases in that order.
• Assume for simplicity that the validation and write phase occur together, atomically 
and serially
• i.e., only one transaction executes validation/write at a time. 
• Also called as optimistic concurrency control since transaction executes fully in the 
hope that all will go well during validation.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 43

Validation-Based Protocol
• Each transaction Ti has 3 timestamps
• Start(Ti) : the time when Ti started its execution
• Validation(Ti): the time when Ti entered its validation phase
• Finish(Ti) : the time when Ti finished its write phase
• Serializability order is determined by timestamp given at validation time; this is done 
to increase concurrency. 
• Thus, TS(Ti) is given the value of Validation(Ti).
•This protocol is useful and gives greater degree of concurrency if probability of 
conflicts is low. 
• because the serializability order is not pre-decided, and
• relatively few transactions will have to be rolled back.

• If for all Ti with TS (Ti) < TS (Tj) either one of the following condition holds:
• finish(Ti) < start(Tj) 
• start(Tj) < finish(Ti) < validation(Tj) and the set of data items written by Ti does not 
intersect with the set of data items read by Tj. 
• then validation succeeds and Tj can be committed. Otherwise, validation fails and Tj
is aborted.

Necessary Conditions of Deadlock 
For a deadlock to occur in a DBMS, all four conditions must be true simultaneously:
1. Mutual Exclusion
Only one transaction can hold a resource (lock) at a time . Other transactions must wait if 
the resource is already locked 
2. Hold and Wait
A transaction is holding one resource .While waiting for another resource held by another 
transaction 
3. No Preemption
Resources (locks) cannot be forcibly taken away .They are released only by the transaction 
itself
4. Circular Wait
A cycle of transactions exists . Each transaction is waiting for a resource held by the next
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 50

Deadlock Handling
There are three main approaches to handle deadlocks. 
•The first is deadlock prevention, where the system ensures that deadlocks never occur by 
restricting how locks are requested. Techniques like wait-die and wound-wait use timestamps to 
decide which transaction should wait or be rolled back.
•The second approach is deadlock avoidance, where the system checks whether granting a lock 
request will lead to a deadlock. If there is a risk, the request is denied. This approach is less 
commonly used due to its complexity.
•The third approach is deadlock detection and recovery. In this method, the system allows 
deadlocks to occur but periodically checks for them using a wait-for graph. If a cycle is found, 
one transaction is selected as a victim and rolled back to break the deadlock.

•Wait-Die Protocol
•Wound-Wait Protocol
Both are timestamp-based deadlock prevention algorithms
When multiple transactions run together, they may get into a deadlock (each waiting for the 
other forever).
•These protocols prevent deadlock before it happens
They decide: who should wait and who should be aborted

Wait-Die Scheme
In this protocol, if a transaction requests to lock a resource (data item), which is already held 
with a conflicting lock by another transaction, then one of the two possibilities may occur − 
• If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) − that is Ti, which is requesting a conflicting lock, is older than Tj − then Ti is 
allowed to wait until the data-item is available. 
• If TS(Ti) > TS(tj) − that is Ti is younger than Tj − then Ti dies. Ti is restarted later with a random 
delay but with the same timestamp. 
•This scheme allows the older transaction to wait but kills the younger one.

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 54
Assume two transactions:
T1 with timestamp TS(T1) = 5 (older) 
T2 with timestamp TS(T2) = 10 (younger) 
Smaller timestamp = older transaction
Case 1: Older transaction requests a lock 
(WAIT)
•T2 already holds a lock on data item X
•Now T1 requests a lock on X
Check condition:
•TS(T1) < TS(T2) → 5 < 10 
• (T1 is older) 
According to Wait-Die:
•T1 is allowed to WAIT
Result:
•T1 waits until T2 releases the lock 
•No transaction is killed
Case 2: Younger transaction requests a lock 
(DIE)
•T1 already holds a lock on data item X
•Now T2 requests a lock on X
Check condition:
•TS(T2) > TS(T1) → 10 > 5 
•(T2 is younger) 
According to Wait-Die:
•T2 will DIE (abort)
Result:
•T2 is rolled back 
•Later, T2 restarts with same timestamp (10)

Wound-Wait Scheme
In this protocol, if a transaction requests to lock a resource (data item), which is already held 
with conflicting lock by some another transaction, one of the two possibilities may occur −
• If TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), then Ti forces Tj to be rolled back − that is Ti wounds Tj. Tj is restarted later 
with a random delay but with the same timestamp.
• If TS(Ti) > TS(Tj), then Ti is forced to wait until the resource is available. 
This protocol, allows the younger transaction to wait; but when an older transaction requests an 
item held by a younger one, the older transaction forces the younger one to abort and release 
the item.

Deadlock Detection
• Deadlocks can be described as a wait-for graph, which consists of a pair G = 
(V,E),
◦ V is a set of vertices (all the transactions in the system)
◦ E is a set of edges; each element is an ordered pair Ti →Tj
.
• If Ti → Tj is in E, then there is a directed edge from Ti to Tj, implying that Ti is 
waiting for Tj to release a data item.
• When Ti requests a data item currently being held by Tj, then the edge Ti → Tj is 
inserted in the wait-for graph. This edge is removed only when Tj is no longer 
holding a data item needed by Ti.

• The system is in a deadlock state if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle. 
• Must invoke a deadlock-detection algorithm periodically to look for cycles.

Deadlock Recovery
• When deadlock is detected:
• Some transaction will have to rolled back (made a victim) to break deadlock. Select 
that transaction as victim that will incur minimum cost.
• Rollback -- determine how far to roll back transaction.
• Total rollback: Abort the transaction and then restart it.
• More effective to roll back transaction only as far as necessary to break deadlock.
• Starvation happens if same transaction is always chosen as victim. Include the 
number of rollbacks in the cost factor to avoid starvation.

Stable Storage Implementation
•Failure during data transfer can still result in inconsistent copies: Block transfer can 
result in
• Successful completion
• Partial failure: destination block has incorrect information
• Total failure: destination block was never updated
•Protecting storage media from failure during data transfer (one solution):
• Execute output operation as follows (assuming two copies of each block):
1. Write the information onto the first physical block.
2. When the first write successfully completes, write the same information onto the second physical 
block.
3. The output is completed only after the second write successfully completes.

Stable Storage Implementation
•Protecting storage media from failure during data transfer:
•Copies of a block may differ due to failure during output operation. To recover from failure:
•1. First find inconsistent blocks:
1. Expensive solution: Compare the two copies of every disk block.
2. Better solution:
Record in-progress disk writes on non-volatile storage (Nonvolatile RAM or special area of disk).
Use this information during recovery to find blocks that may be inconsistent, and only compare 
copies of these.
Used in hardware RAID systems
•2. If either copy of an inconsistent block is detected to have an error (bad checksum), 
overwrite it by the other copy. If both have no error, but are different, overwrite the second 
block by the first block.

Shadow Paging
•Shadow Paging is alternative to log-based recovery.
•This scheme is useful if transactions execute serially. 
•It ensures ACID properties (atomicity and durability) without using logs
•It maintains two page tables.
1. Shadow Page Table (original, stable state) 
2. Current Page Table (for active updates). 
•Updates are made on a new copy, not on the original.
•It enables fast, instantaneous recovery by discarding the current table upon 
failure and switching tables upon commit.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 16

Shadow Paging
•Store the shadow page table in nonvolatile storage, such that state of the database 
prior to transaction execution may be recovered.
• Shadow page table is never modified during execution.
•To start with, both the page tables are identical. 
•Only current page table is used for data item accesses during execution of the 
transaction. 
•Whenever any page is about to be written for the first time
• A copy of this page is made onto an unused page.
• The current page table is then made to point to the copy
• The update is performed on the copy

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 18

Shadow Paging
Key Components and Working:
•Two Tables: When a transaction starts, the current page table is a copy of the 
shadow page table. Both point to the same pages on the disk.
•Out-of-Place Updates: When a page is modified, a new block is allocated on the 
disk, and the modification is written there. The current page table points to this 
new block, while the shadow page table still points to the old, unmodified block.
•Commit: To commit, the current page table becomes the new shadow page table, 
and the old disk blocks are freed.
•Abort/Recovery: If the transaction fails, the current page table is discarded, and 
the shadow table remains, effectively reversing changes without undo operations.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 19

Shadow Paging
Advantages:
Fast Recovery: No UNDO or REDO operations are required.
No Overhead: Eliminates the need for writing log records to the disk continuously. 
Disadvantages:
Data Fragmentation: Pages become scattered on the disk over time, reducing 
performance.
High Commit Cost: Committing requires updating the entire page table and clearing old 
pages, which is inefficient.
Concurrency Issues: Difficult to manage multiple concurrent transactions compared to 
log-based techniques

Checkpoints
• Redoing/undoing all transactions recorded in the log can be very slow
• Processing the entire log is time-consuming if the system has run for a long time
• We might unnecessarily redo transactions which have already output their updates to 
the database.
• Streamline recovery procedure by periodically performing checkpointing
•1. Output all log records currently residing in main memory onto stable storage.
•2. Output all modified buffer blocks to the disk.
•3. Write a log record < checkpoint L> onto stable storage where L is a list of all 
transactions active at the time of checkpoint.
•4. All updates are stopped while doing checkpointing
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 43

Checkpoints
•During recovery we need to consider only the most recent transaction Ti that started before 
the checkpoint, and transactions that started after Ti.
• Scan backwards from end of log to find the most recent <checkpoint L> record
• Only transactions that are in L or started after the checkpoint need to be redone or undone
• Transactions that committed or aborted before the checkpoint already have all their updates 
output to stable storage.
• Some earlier part of the log may be needed for undo operations
• Continue scanning backwards till a record <Ti start> is found for every transaction Ti in L.
• Parts of log prior to earliest <Ti start> record above are not needed for recovery, and can be 
erased whenever desired.

(updates already output to disk

• T2 and T3 redone.
• T4 undone

•Logging (during normal operation):
• <Ti start> at transaction start
• <Ti, Xj, V1, V2> for each update, and
• <Ti commit> at transaction end
• Transaction rollback (during normal operation)
• Let Ti be the transaction to be rolled back
• Scan log backwards from the end, and for each log record of Ti of the form <Ti, Xj, V1, V2>
• Perform the undo by writing V1 to Xj,
• Write a log record <Ti , Xj, V1>
• such log records are called compensation log records
• Once the record <Ti start> is found stop the scan and write the log record <Ti abort>

4. Now permit transactions to proceed with their actions

oblocks should not be updated while being output

• ARIES- Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics

Physiological redo
• Affected page is physically identified, action within page can be logical
• Used to reduce logging overheads
• e.g. when a record is deleted and all other records have to be moved to fill hole
• Physiological redo can log just the record deletion
• Physical redo would require logging of old and new values for much of the page
• Requires page to be output to disk atomically
• Easy to achieve with hardware RAID, also supported by some disk systems
• Incomplete page output can be detected by checksum techniques

ARIES Recovery Algorithm
Analysis pass: determines

• Which pages were dirty (disk version not up to date) at time of crash

Redo pass

ARIES Recovery Algorithm
Undo pass
• Rolls back all incomplete transactions

Analysis pass
• Starts from last complete checkpoint log record
• Reads DirtyPageTable from log record
• Sets RedoLSN = min of RecLSNs of all pages in DirtyPageTable
• In case no pages are dirty, RedoLSN = checkpoint record’s LSN
• Sets undo-list = list of transactions in checkpoint log record
• Reads LSN of last log record for each transaction in undo-list from checkpoint log record
• Scans forward from checkpoint

record

• Keeps track of last log record for each transaction in undo-list

Analysis pass

ARIES Algorithm
Redo pass: Repeats history by replaying every action not already reflected in the page on 
disk, as follows:
• Scans forward from RedoLSN. Whenever an update log record is found:
1. If the page is not in DirtyPageTable or the LSN of the log record is less than the 
RecLSN of the page in DirtyPageTable, then skip the log record.
2. Otherwise fetch the page from disk. If the PageLSN of the page fetched from disk is less 
than the LSN of the log record, redo the log record

Files
 The database is stored as a collection of files. 
 Each file is a sequence of records. 
 A record is a sequence of fields.
 Record is a basic unit of information for computer and file.
 For e.g., Student_name, Address, Phone_no are fields of STUDENT record.
 A set of logically related records form a file.
 File system: The structure and logical rules used to manage the groups of 
information and their names.

Files
One approach
 Assume record size is fixed
 Each file has records of one particular type only
 Different files are used for different relations.
 We assume that records are smaller than a disk block
Files
Files

Operations on Files
 In DBMS, two fundamental types of operations are performed on files:
 1. Retrieval (finding and reading records)
 2. Updation (inserting, deleting or modifying records)
 Operations can be record-at-a-time (process one record) or set-at-a-time 
(find all matching records at once).

Operations on Files
System Control Operations
 These operations handle the setup, closing, and background optimization of 
files.
 Open: Allocates buffer memory and prepares the file for read or write 
modes.
 Close: Releases the allocated memory buffer, saves remaining changes, 
and revokes access to the file.
 Reset: Re-positions the active file pointer back to the very first record.
 Reorganize: Re-arranges the internal layout of records. This reclaims wasted 
storage space left behind by deleted entries and improves performance.

Operations on Files
Retrieval Operations
 These operations read records from the file based on a specific selection 
condition.
 Find (or Locate): Searches for the first record in the file that satisfies a specific 
selection condition. It sets the file pointer to that record.
 FindNext: Finds the next consecutive record in the file matching the criteria. 
It advances the pointer forward.
 Read (or Get): Copies the current record from the main memory block buffer 
into the program's variables.
 FindAll: Retrieves all data records that match a given condition 
simultaneously.
 FindOrdered: Fetches matching data records sorted by a specified key or 
field.

Operations on Files
Update Operations
 These operations change the data values or the physical structure of the file 
on disk.
 Insert: Adds a new record to the file. The system locates the appropriate 
storage block, loads it into the buffer, writes the record, and saves it back to 
disk.
 Delete: Marks or removes a specific record from the file. It updates the 
physical storage to reflect that the data space is now vacant.
 Modify (or Update): Changes the specific field values of an existing record. 
The block is updated in the memory buffer before being written back to disk.

Organization of Records in Files
1. Heap – record can be placed anywhere in the file where there is space.
2. Sequential – store records in sequential order, based on the value of the 
search key of each record.
3. Multitable clustering – records of several different relations can be stored in 
the same file.
• Motivation: store related records on the same block to minimize I/O
4. B+-tree file organization
• Ordered storage even with inserts/deletes
5. Hashing – a hash function computed on search key; the result specifies in 
which block of the file the record should be placed.

Hashing
 Hashing is a technique in DBMS that is used to search for records in 
databases.
 Particularly useful in very large databases where indexing technique 
becomes inefficient.
 Hashing is an efficient technique to directly search the location of desired 
data on the disk without using an index structure. 
 Data is stored in the data blocks whose address is generated by using a 
hash function.
Hashing

Hashing
Components of Hashing
1.Key: Input data to be stored or retrieved.
2.Hash Function: Converts the key into a unique index.
3.Hash Table: Array storing data at unique indices for efficient lookup.
Hashing

Hashing
Terminologies used:
1. Hash Table
 The total number of data records in the database determines the size of a 
hash table, which is an array or data structure. 
 The precise location of a data record stored in each memory location in a 
hash table is referred to as a “bucket” or hash index and is accessible via a 
hash function.

Hashing
Terminologies used:
2. Bucket
 A bucket is a unit of storage containing one or more entries (a bucket is 
typically a disk block).
 In the hash table where the data record is stored, a bucket is a memory 
index.
 Entries with different search-key values may be mapped to the same 
bucket; thus, the entire bucket has to be searched sequentially to locate an 
entry. 
 In a hash index, buckets store entries with pointers to records.
 In a hash file-organization buckets store records.

Hashing
Terminologies used:
3. Hash Function
 we obtain the bucket of an entry from its search-key value using a hash 
function
 A hash function is an algorithm or mathematical equation that computes 
the hash index as the output after receiving the main key of one data 
record as input. 
 The hash function is a mapping function that maps all the sets of search keys 
to the actual record address OR Hash function h is a function from the set of 
all search-key values K to the set of all bucket addresses B.. 
 Generally, the hash function uses the primary key to generate the hash 
index.
 Hash function is used to locate entries for access, insertion as well as 
deletion.

 Generally, the hash function uses the primary key to generate the hash

3. Hash Function
 An ideal hash function is uniform, i.e., each bucket is assigned the same 
number of search-key values from the set of all possible values.
 An ideal hash function is random, so each bucket will have the same 
number of records assigned to it irrespective of the actual distribution of 
search-key values in the file.

Hashing
Static Hashing:
 maps search keys to a fixed number of addressable buckets
 uses a consistent hash function, ensures the database size remains constant.
 when a search-key value is provided, the hash function always computes 
the same address.
 For example, if we want to generate an address for STUDENT_ID = 104 using 
a mod (5) hash function, it always results in the same bucket address 4. 
There will not be any changes to the bucket address here. 
 Hence, the number of data buckets in the memory for this static hashing 
remain constant throughout.

Bucket overflow or Collision
 Suppose that we want to insert some new records into the file, but the data 
bucket address generated by the hash function is not empty or the data 
already exists in that address. 
 This situation in static hashing is called bucket overflow or collision.
 Bucket overflow can occur because of:
 Insufficient buckets
 Skew in distribution of records. This can occur due to two reasons:
 multiple records have same search-key value
 chosen hash function produces non-uniform distribution of key values

respectively. 
 This method of storing considers only part of this address - especially only the 
first bit to store the data.

Indexing
 Database Management Systems (DBMS) handle large volumes of data that 
need to be accessed quickly and efficiently.
 Indexing is a technique used in DBMS to speed up the search for specific 
records within the database. 
 It plays a crucial role in enhancing query performance and alleviating 
system load.
 Indexing in DBMS is a data structure technique used to speed up the 
retrieval of records from a table. 
 It creates a separate, smaller structure (an “index”) that stores key attributes 
from a table, allowing the database to locate rows without scanning the 
entire dataset.
Indexing

Indexing
Advantages of Indexing in DBMS
1.Faster Data Retrieval: Indices allow quick access to records without
scanning the entire table.
2.Improved Query Performance: Enhances the efficiency of SELECT queries,
JOINs, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY operations.
3.Support for Uniqueness: Enforces unique constraints on columns like primary
keys to maintain data integrity.
4.Reduced I/O Operations: Minimizes disk access by providing direct pointers
to data locations.
5.Efficient Sorting: Maintains data in sorted order, speeding up ORDER BY and
range queries.

Indexing
Disadvantages of Indexing in DBMS
1.Slower Write Operations: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE become slightly slower
because indices must be updated.
2.Additional Storage Required: Indices consume extra disk space depending
on their type and size.
3.Maintenance Overhead: Indices need periodic updates, which adds
management complexity.
4.Over-Indexing Risk: Too many indices can degrade performance instead of
improving it.
5.Not Always Suitable: For small tables or rarely queried columns, indices may
offer minimal benefit.
Indexing

Single-level Indices
 A single-level index is an auxiliary file that makes it more efficient to search 
for a record in the data file.
 The index is usually specified on one field of the file (although it could be 
specified on several fields)
 One form of an index is a file of entries <field value, pointer to record>, 
which is ordered by field value
 The index is called an access path on the field.

Single-level Indices
 The index file usually occupies considerably less disk blocks than the data 
file because its entries are much smaller
 A binary search on the index yields a pointer to the file record
 Indices can also be characterized as dense or sparse
 A dense index has an index entry for every search key value (and hence 
every record) in the data file.
 A sparse (or nondense) index, on the other hand, has index entries for only 
some of the search values.

Single-level Indices
Dense Index Files
 Dense index — Index record appears for every search-key value in the file.
 E.g. index on ID attribute of instructor relation

Single-level Indices
Dense Index Files
 Dense index on dept_name, with instructor file sorted on dept_name

Single-level Indices
Sparse Index Files
 Sparse Index: contains index records for only some search-key values.
 Applicable when records are sequentially ordered on search-key
 To locate a record with search-key value K we:
 • Find index record with largest search-key value < K
 • Search file sequentially starting at the record to which the index record points
 Compared to dense indices:
 • Less space and less maintenance overhead for insertions and deletions.
 • Generally slower than dense index for locating records.

1. Primary Index
2. Clustering Index

Types of Single-level Indices
Primary Index
 Defined on an ordered data file
 The data file is ordered on a key field
 Includes one index entry for each block in the data file; the index entry has 
the key field value for the first record in the block, which is called the block 
anchor
 A similar scheme can use the last record in a block.
 A primary index is a nondense (sparse) index, since it includes an entry for 
each disk block of the data file and the keys of its anchor record rather 
than for every search value.

Types of Single-level Indices
Primary Index

Types of Single-level Indices
Clustering Index
 Defined on an ordered data file
 The data file is ordered on a non-key field unlike primary index, which 
requires that the ordering field of the data file have a distinct value for 
each record.
 Includes one index entry for each distinct value of the field; the index entry 
points to the first data block that contains records with that field value.
 It is another example of nondense index where Insertion and Deletion is 
relatively straightforward with a clustering index.

Secondary Index
 A secondary index provides a secondary means of accessing a file for which 
some primary access already exists.
 The secondary index may be on a field which is a candidate key and has a 
unique value in every record, or a non-key with duplicate values.
 The index is an ordered file with two fields.
 The first field is of the same data type as some non-ordering field of the data file 
that is an indexing field.
 The second field is either a block pointer or a record pointer.
 There can be many secondary indices (and hence, indexing fields) for the 
same file.
 Includes one entry for each record in the data file; hence, it is a dense index

Types of Single-level Indices
Properties of Index Types

Hash Indices
 Hashing can be used not only for file organization, but also for index￾structure creation. 
 A hash index organizes the search keys, with their associated record 
pointers, into a hash file structure.
 Strictly speaking, hash indices are always secondary indices
 If the file itself is organized using hashing, a separate primary hash index on 
it using the same search-key is unnecessary.
 However, we use the term hash index to refer to both secondary index 
structures and hash organized files.

Multi-level Indices
Problem with Single-level indexing
 Single-level indexing consists of a single list of key-pointer pairs. 
 It performs well with small datasets, allowing quick lookups. 
 However, as the data size increases, this simple index becomes less efficient 
because it must scan through more entries sequentially.

Multi-level Indices
Solution
 Because a single-level index is an ordered file, we can create a primary 
index to the index itself;
 In this case, the original index file is called the first-level index and the index 
to the index is called the second-level index.
 We can repeat the process, creating a third, fourth, ..., top level until all 
entries of the top-level fit in one disk block
 A multi-level index can be created for any type of first level index (primary, 
secondary, clustering) as long as the first-level index consists of more than 
one disk block.
 Thus, multi-level indexing arranges indices in a hierarchical structure. 
 This approach is highly effective for large datasets, as it minimizes disk 
access and greatly improves lookup speed.
Multi-level Indices

Multi-level Indices
 Such a multi-level index is a form of search tree.
 However, insertion and deletion of new index entries is a severe problem 
because every level of the index is an ordered file.

Multi-level Indices
 A Node in a Search Tree with Pointers to Subtrees below It

Multi-level Indices
A search tree of order p = 3.

Dynamic Multilevel Indices Using B-Trees 
and B+-Trees
 Most multi-level indices use B-tree or B+-tree data structures because of the 
insertion and deletion problem
 This leaves space in each tree node (disk block) to allow for new index 
entries
 These data structures are variations of search trees that allow efficient 
insertion and deletion of new search values.
 In B-Tree and B+-Tree data structures, each node corresponds to a disk 
block
 Each node is kept between half-full and completely full.

Dynamic Multilevel Indices Using B-Trees 
and B+-Trees
 An insertion into a node that is not full is quite efficient.
 If a node is full the insertion causes a split into two nodes.
 Splitting may propagate to other tree levels.
 A deletion is quite efficient if a node does not become less than half full.
 If a deletion causes a node to become less than half full, it must be merged 
with neighboring nodes.

Difference between B-tree and B+-tree
 In a B-tree, pointers to data records exist at all levels of the tree.
 In a B+-tree, all pointers to data records exists at the leaf-level nodes.
 A B+-tree can have less levels (or higher capacity of search values) than 
the corresponding B-tree.

 An index on multiple keys is a database structure where a single index is

 This approach optimizes query performance when search filters (WHERE

Query Processing
 Query processing refers to the range of activities involved in extracting data 
from a database. 
 The activities include 
 translation of queries in high-level database languages into expressions 
that can be used at the physical level of the file system, 
 a variety of query-optimizing transformations, 
 and actual evaluation of queries.

Basic Steps in Query Processing
1. Parsing and translation
2. Optimization
3. Evaluation

Basic Steps in Query Processing
Parsing and translation
 translate the query into its internal form. This is then translated into relational 
algebra.
 Parser checks syntax, verifies relations.
 The system constructs a parse-tree representation of the query, which it then 
translates into a relational-algebra expression.
Evaluation
 The query-execution engine takes a query-evaluation plan, executes that 
plan, and returns the answers to the query.

Basic Steps in Query Processing
Optimization
 A relational algebra expression may have many equivalent expressions
 E.g., consider the query:
 select salary
 from instructor
 where salary < 75000;
 Equivalent relational-algebra expressions:
 salary<75000(salary(instructor))
 salary(salary<75000(instructor))
 Each relational algebra operation can be evaluated using one of several 
different algorithms
 Correspondingly, a relational-algebra expression can be evaluated in many 
ways.

Basic Steps in Query Processing
Optimization
 To evaluate a query, we also need not to annotate it with instructions 
specifying how to evaluate each operation. 
 Annotations may state the algorithm to be used for a specific operation or 
the particular index or indices to use. 
 A relational-algebra operation annotated with instructions on how to 
evaluate it is called an evaluation primitive. 
 A sequence of primitive operations that can be used to evaluate a query is 
a query-execution plan or query-evaluation plan.
 E.g.,:
 Use an index on salary to find instructors with salary < 75000,
 Or perform complete relation scan and discard instructors with salary 
75000.

 Many factors contribute to time cost

 Cost can be measured based on 
 response time, i.e. total elapsed time for answering query, or

 We ignore CPU costs for simplicity

Pipelining
 In demand driven or lazy evaluation
 system repeatedly requests next tuple from top level operation
 Each operation requests next tuple from children operations as required, in order to output its 
next tuple
 In between calls, operation has to maintain “state” so it knows what to return next
 In producer-driven or eager pipelining
 Operators produce tuples eagerly and pass them up to their parents
 Buffer maintained between operators, child puts tuples in buffer, parent removes tuples from 
buffer
 if buffer is full, child waits till there is space in the buffer, and then generates more tuples
 System schedules operations that have space in output buffer and can process more input 
tuples
 Alternative name: pull and push models of pipelining

 Query optimization is the process of selecting the most efficient query￾evaluation plan from among the many strategies usually possible for 
processing a given query.
 Query Optimization is all about finding the query plan that minimizes the 
number of I/Os it takes to execute the query.
 Query optimization helps choose the most efficient plan by comparing 
different execution methods to find the one with the lowest cost. 
 The goal of query optimization is to reduce the system resources required to 
fulfill a query, and ultimately provide the user with the correct result set 
faster.

 Steps in cost-based query optimization
1. Generate logically equivalent expressions using equivalence rules

3. Choose the cheapest plan based on estimated cost

Choice of Evaluation Plans
Cost-based optimization
 A cost-based optimizer explores the space of all query-evaluation plans that 
are equivalent to the given query, and chooses the one with the least 
estimated cost.
 Consider finding the best join-order for r1 ⨝ r2 ⨝

.

least-cost join order for any subset of {r1
, r2

and stored for future use.

Left-deep join trees

Heuristic Optimization
 Cost-based optimization is expensive, even with dynamic programming.
 Systems may use heuristics to reduce the number of choices that must be 
made in a cost-based fashion.
 Heuristic optimization transforms the query-tree by using a set of rules that 
typically (but not in all cases) improve execution performance:
 Perform selection early (reduces the number of tuples)
 Perform projection early (reduces the number of attributes)
 Perform most restrictive selection and join operations (i.e., with smallest result 
size) before other similar operations.
 Some systems use only heuristics, others combine heuristics with partial cost￾based optimization.

Database Security
● The data stored in a DBMS is often vital to the business interests of the 
organization and is regarded as a corporate asset. 
● In addition to protecting the intrinsic value of the data, corporations must 
consider ways to ensure privacy and controlled access to data.
Database Security

Database Security Issues
Types of Security
● Legal and ethical issues- regarding the right to access certain information
● Policy issues eg: credit ratings and personal medical records
● System-related issues eg: security function at hardware, OS level or DBMS 
level
● The need to identify multiple security levels eg: top secret, secret, 
confidential

Database Security Issues
Threats to databases
● Loss of integrity
○ Integrity is lost if unauthorized changes are made to the 
data by either intentional or accidental acts.
○ could result in inaccuracy, fraud, or erroneous decisions.
● Loss of availability
○ Loss of availability occurs when the user or program cannot 
access the data objects.
● Loss of confidentiality
○ Unauthorized, unanticipated, or unintentional disclosure 
could result in loss of public confidence, embarrassment, or 
legal action against the organization.

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
● DBMS alone cannot be responsible for maintaining the confidentiality, 
integrity, and availability of the data.
● Rather, the database works as part of a network of services, including 
applications, Web servers, firewalls, SSL terminators, and security 
monitoring systems.
● So, a database may be compromised even if it would have been perfectly 
secure on its own merits.
● Four control measures to protect databases against the threats: access 
control, inference control, flow control, and encryption.

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
● A DBMS typically includes a database security and authorization 
subsystem that is responsible for ensuring the security portions of a 
database against unauthorized access.
● Two types of database security mechanisms:
a. Discretionary security mechanisms
b. Mandatory security mechanisms

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
● Four control measures to protect databases against the threats:
○ Access control
○ Inference control
○ Flow control
○ Encryption

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
Access Control
● The security mechanism of a DBMS must include provisions for restricting 
access to the database as a whole
● This function is called access control and is handled by creating user 
accounts and passwords to control login process by the DBMS.

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
Inference Control
● The security problem associated with databases is that of controlling the 
access to a statistical database, which is used to provide statistical 
information or summaries of values based on various criteria.
● The countermeasures to statistical database security problem is called 
inference control measures.

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
Flow Control
● Another security is that of flow control, which prevents information from 
flowing in such a way that it reaches unauthorized users.
● Channels that are pathways for information to flow implicitly in ways that 
violate the security policy of an organization are called covert channels.

Database Security Issues
Database Security: Not an Isolated Concern
Encryption
● A final security issue is data encryption, which is used to protect 
sensitive data (such as credit card numbers) that is being transmitted via 
some type communication network.
● The data is encoded using some encoding algorithm.
● An unauthorized user who access encoded data will have difficulty 
deciphering it, but authorized users are given decoding or decrypting 
algorithms (or keys) to decipher data.

Database Security Issues
Four control measures

Database Security and the DBA
● The database administrator (DBA) is the central authority for managing a 
database system.
● The DBA’s responsibilities include:
○ granting privileges to users who need to use the system
○ classifying users and data in accordance with the policy of the organization
● The DBA is responsible for the overall security of the database system
Database Security and the DBA

Database Security and the DBA
● The DBA has a DBA account in the DBMS.
● Sometimes it is called a system or a superuser account.
● This account provides powerful capabilities such as:
1. Account creation
2. Privilege granting
3. Privilege revocation
4. Security level assignment
● Action 1 is access control, whereas 2 and 3 are discretionary and 4 is 
used to control mandatory authorization

Authorization
Access Protection, User Accounts, and Database Audits
● Whenever a person or group of persons need to access a database 
system, the individual or group must first apply for a user account.
● The DBA will then create a new account id and password for the user if 
he/she deems there is a legitimate need to access the database
● The user must log in to the DBMS by entering account id and password 
whenever database access is needed.

Authorization
Access Protection, User Accounts, and Database Audits
● The database system must also keep track of all operations on the 
database that are applied by a certain user throughout each login session.
● To keep a record of all updates applied to the database and of the 
particular user who applied each update, we can modify system log, 
which includes an entry for each operation applied to the database that 
may be required for recovery from a transaction failure or system crash.

Authorization
Access Protection, User Accounts, and Database Audits
● If any tampering with the database is suspected, a database audit is 
performed
● A database audit consists of reviewing the log to examine all accesses and 
operations applied to the database during a certain time period.
● A database log that is used mainly for security purposes is sometimes 
called an audit trail.

Authorization
Sensitive Data and Types of Disclosures
Sensitivity of data is a measure of the importance assigned to the data by its owner for the 
purpose of denoting its need for protection.
Several factors can cause data to be classified as sensitive:
1. Inherently sensitive: The value of the data itself may be so revealing or confidential 
that it becomes sensitive—for example, a person’s salary or whether a patient has 
HIV/AIDS.
2. From a sensitive source: The source of the data may indicate a need for secrecy—for 
example, an informer whose identity must be kept secret.
3. Declared sensitive: The owner of the data may have explicitly declared it as sensitive.
4. A sensitive attribute or sensitive record: The particular attribute or record may have 
been declared sensitive—for example, the salary attribute of an employee or the salary 
history record in a personnel database.
5. Sensitive in relation to previously disclosed data: Some data may not be sensitive 
by itself but will become sensitive in the presence of some other data—for example, 
the exact latitude and longitude information for a location where some previously 
recorded event happened that was later deemed sensitive.

Authorization
Sensitive Data and Types of Disclosures
Several factors must be considered before deciding whether it is safe to reveal 
the data. 
The three most important factors are data availability, access acceptability, 
and authenticity assurance.
1. Data availability: If a user is updating a field, then this field becomes 
inaccessible and other users should not be able to view this data 
(temporarily-concurrency control).
2. Access acceptability: Data should only be revealed to authorized users.
3. Authenticity assurance: Before granting access, certain external 
characteristics about the user may also be considered. For example, a 
user may only be permitted access during working hours.

Authorization
Security versus Precision
● Security: Means of ensuring that data is kept safe from corruption and 
that access to it is suitably controlled. To provide security means to 
disclose only nonsensitive data and to reject any query that references a 
sensitive field.
● Precision: To protect all sensitive data while disclosing or making 
available as much nonsensitive data as possible.
The ideal combination is to maintain perfect security with maximum precision.

Authorization
Relationship between Information Security and Information Privacy
● Security: Security in information technology refers to many aspects of 
protecting a system from unauthorized use, including authentication of 
users, information encryption, access control, firewall policies, and 
intrusion detection.
● Privacy: privacy is the ability of individuals to control the terms under 
which their personal information is acquired and used.
Security involves technology to ensure that information is appropriately 
protected. Security is a required building block for privacy.
Privacy involves mechanisms to support compliance with some basic 
principles and other explicitly stated policies.
Trust, relates to both security and privacy and is seen as increasing when it is 
perceived that both security and privacy are provided for.

Discretionary Access Control
Discretionary security mechanisms:
● These are used to grant privileges to users.
● The privileges include the capability to access specific data files, records, 
or fields in a specified mode. 
● The mode may be either read, insert, delete, or update.
The typical method of enforcing discretionary access control in a database 
system is based on the granting and revoking privileges.

Discretionary Access Control
Types of Discretionary Privileges
● The account level:
○ At this level, the DBA specifies the particular privileges that each account holds 
independently of the relations in the database.
● The relation level (or table level):
○ At this level, the DBA can control the privilege to access each individual 
relation or view in the database.

Discretionary Access Control
Types of Discretionary Privileges
● The second level of privileges applies to the relation level.
○ This includes base relations and virtual (view) relations.
● The granting and revoking of privileges generally follow an authorization 
model for discretionary privileges known as the access matrix model 
where 
○ The rows of a matrix M represents subjects (users, accounts, programs)
○ The columns represent objects (relations, records, columns, views, 
operations).
○ Each position M(i,j) in the matrix represents the types of privileges (read, 
write, update) that subject i holds on object j.

Discretionary Access Control
Types of Discretionary Privileges
● The mechanism of views is an important discretionary authorization 
mechanism in its own right. For example,
● If the owner A of a relation R wants another account B to be able to 
retrieve only some fields of R, then A can create a view V of R that 
includes only those attributes and then grant SELECT on V to B.
● The same applies to limiting B to retrieving only certain tuples of R; a view 
V’ can be created by defining the view by means of a query that selects 
only those tuples from R that A wants to allow B to access.

Discretionary Access Control
Revoking Privileges
● In some cases, it is desirable to grant a privilege to a user temporarily. 
● For example, 
● The owner of a relation may want to grant the SELECT privilege to a user 
for a specific task and then revoke that privilege once the task is 
completed.
● Hence, a mechanism for revoking privileges is needed. 
● In SQL, a REVOKE command is included for the purpose of canceling 
privileges.

Discretionary Access Control
Propagation of Privileges using the GRANT OPTION
● Whenever the owner A of a relation R grants a privilege on R to another 
account B, privilege can be given to B with or without the GRANT OPTION.
● If the GRANT OPTION is given, this means that B can also grant that 
privilege on R to other accounts. 
● Suppose that B is given the GRANT OPTION by A and that B then grants 
the privilege on R to a third account C, also with GRANT OPTION. 
● In this way, privileges on R can propagate to other accounts without the 
knowledge of the owner of R.

Discretionary Access Control
Propagation of Privileges using the GRANT OPTION
● If the owner account A now revokes the privilege granted to B, all the 
privileges that B propagated based on that privilege should 
automatically be revoked by the system.

Discretionary Access Control
Example- Grant and Revoke
● Suppose that the DBA creates four accounts
○ A1, A2, A3, A4
● and wants only A1 to be able to create base relations. Then the DBA must 
issue the following GRANT command in SQL
GRANT CREATETAB TO A1;
● In SQL2 the same effect can be accomplished by having the DBA issue a 
CREATE SCHEMA command as follows:
CREATE SCHEMA EXAMPLE AUTHORIZATION A1;

Discretionary Access Control
Example- Grant and Revoke
● User account A1 can create tables under the schema called EXAMPLE.
● Suppose that A1 creates the two base relations EMPLOYEE and 
DEPARTMENT
● A1 is then owner of these two relations and hence all the relation 
privileges on each of them.
● Suppose that A1 wants to grant A2 the privilege to insert and delete 
tuples in both of these relations, but A1 does not want A2 to be able to 
propagate these privileges to additional accounts:
GRANT INSERT, DELETE ON
EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT TO A2;

Discretionary Access Control
Example- Grant and Revoke
● Schemas for the two relations- EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT

Discretionary Access Control
Example- Grant and Revoke
● Suppose that A1 wants to allow A3 to retrieve information from either of the 
two tables and also to be able to propagate the SELECT privilege to other 
accounts.
● A1 can issue the command:
GRANT SELECT ON EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT 
TO A3 WITH GRANT OPTION;
● A3 can grant the SELECT privilege on the EMPLOYEE relation to A4 by issuing:
GRANT SELECT ON EMPLOYEE TO A4;
● Notice that A4 can’t propagate the SELECT privilege because GRANT OPTION 
was not given to A4.

Discretionary Access Control
Example- Grant and Revoke
● Suppose that A1 decides to revoke the SELECT privilege on the EMPLOYEE 
relation from A3; A1 can issue:
REVOKE SELECT ON EMPLOYEE FROM A3;
● The DBMS must now automatically revoke the SELECT privilege on 
EMPLOYEE from A4, too, because A3 granted that privilege to A4 and A3 
does not have the privilege any more.

Discretionary Access Control
Specifying Limits on Propagation of Privileges
● Techniques to limit the propagation of privileges have been developed, 
although they have not yet been implemented in most DBMSs and are not 
a part of SQL.
● Limiting horizontal propagation to an integer number i means that an 
account B given the GRANT OPTION can grant the privilege to at most i 
other accounts.
● Vertical propagation is more complicated; it limits the depth of the 
granting of privileges.

Discretionary Access Control
Example- Specifying Limits on Propagation of Privileges
A1 grants SELECT to A2 on EMPLOYEE relation with:
Horizontal propagation (HP) = 1
Vertical propagation (VP) = 2

Mandatory Access Control
● The discretionary access control techniques of granting and revoking 
privileges on relations has traditionally been the main security 
mechanism for relational database systems.
● This is an all-or-nothing method:
○ A user either has or does not have a certain privilege.
● In many applications, and additional security policy is needed that 
classifies data and users based on security classes. 
● This approach as mandatory access control, would typically be 
combined with the discretionary access control mechanisms.

Mandatory Access Control
● Mandatory Access Control (MAC): ◦ MAC applies to large amounts of 
information requiring strong protect in environments where both the 
system data and users can be classified clearly.
● MAC is a mechanism for enforcing multiple levels of security.
● The commonly used model for multilevel security, is known as the 
Bell-LaPadula model.

Mandatory Access Control
Bell-LaPadula model: Security classes
● Classifies subjects and objects based on security classes. 
● Security class: 
○ Classification level 
○ Clearance
● A subject classification reflects the degree of trust and the application 
area.
● An object classification reflects the sensitivity of the data. 
● Typical security classes are top secret (TS), secret (S), confidential (C), and 
unclassified (U), 
● where TS is the highest level and U the lowest: TS ≥ S ≥ C ≥ U

Mandatory Access Control
Bell-LaPadula model
● Classifies each subject (user, account, program) and object (relation, 
tuple, column, view, operation) into one of the security classifications, TS, 
S, C, or U:
● Clearance (classification) of a subject S as class(S) and to the 
classification of an object O as class(O).

Mandatory Access Control
Bell-LaPadula model
● Two restrictions are enforced on data access based on the subject/object 
classifications:
● Simple security property: A subject S is not allowed read access to an 
object O unless class(S) ≥ class(O).
● A subject S is not allowed to write an object O unless class(S) ≤ class(O). 
This known as the star property (or * property).
